fact_text: As a Spanish (EU) citizen you may take up employment or self-employment in Ireland without an employment permit; no visa is required.
evidence_quote: As an EU citizen you can come to Ireland to look for work, and you can take up employment or self-employment without needing an employment permit. This also applies to citizens of European Economic Area (EEA) and Switzerland.

fact_text: An EU/EEA citizen can stay in Ireland for up to 3 months (6 months if job-seeking) without restriction.
evidence_quote: You can enter Ireland and stay here for up to 3 months (6 months if you are looking for a job) without restriction.

fact_text: To reside in Ireland beyond 3 months an EU citizen must be working (employed/self-employed), be self-sufficient with sickness insurance, or be a student.
evidence_quote: If you plan to stay more than 3 months, you must either:Be working (either employed or self-employed)Have enough money and sickness insurance to support yourself and your family

fact_text: EU/EEA citizens do not need to register with immigration authorities and do not need a residence card to live in Ireland (Ireland has no EU registration certificate system).
evidence_quote: When you come to Ireland, you do not need to register with the immigration authorities and you do not need a residence card to live here.

fact_text: Under EU law a 'worker' is anyone doing genuine and effective paid work under another's direction; there is no minimum earnings or hours threshold to qualify as an EU worker.
evidence_quote: In EU law, a worker is any person who undertakes ‘genuine and effective’ work for which they are paid under the direction of someone else. You do not have to be earning over a particular amount, or working a particular number of hours per week, to be an EU worker.

fact_text: No visa or preclearance is required for EEA/Swiss citizens; Ireland is not in the Schengen Area but a passport or national identity card is needed to enter.
evidence_quote: You do not need a visa or preclearance to come to Ireland if you are a citizen of the EEA or Switzerland.

fact_text: After 5 years living in Ireland as an EU worker or self-employed person, an EU citizen acquires a permanent right of residence.
evidence_quote: If you have lived in Ireland as an EU worker or self-employed person for 5 years, you have a permanent right of residence in Ireland.

fact_text: EU/EEA/Swiss citizens do not have to register with Immigration Service Delivery when moving to Ireland to work.
evidence_quote: You do not have to register with Immigration Service Delivery (the Irish immigration authorities).

fact_text: A PPS Number is applied for online at MyWelfare and requires a basic or verified MyGovID account.
evidence_quote: If you are aged 18 years or older you can apply for a PPS Number for yourself and your child online at MyWelfare.This service is available to customers resident on the island of Ireland and customers resident abroad.To apply online, you will need a basic or verified MyGovID account.

fact_text: For a PPS Number an EU/EEA citizen (other than Irish and UK) provides their current passport or national identity card as evidence of identity.
evidence_quote: If you are an EU/EEA citizen (other than Irish and UK):your current passportORnational identity card

fact_text: A PPS Number application requires evidence of address showing the applicant's name and address, dated no older than 3 months.
evidence_quote: You need to show evidence of your address to get a PPS Number.The document must show your name and address and not be older than 3 months.

fact_text: The PPS Number is the key identifier for accessing social welfare benefits, public services and information in Ireland; it is 7 numbers followed by one or two letters.
evidence_quote: A Personal Public Service (PPS) Number helps you access social welfare benefits, public services and information in Ireland.A PPS Number is always 7 numbers followed by either one or two letters.

fact_text: You are Irish tax resident if present in Ireland for 183 days or more in a tax year, or 280 days or more across the current and preceding tax year combined.
evidence_quote: You are resident in Ireland for tax purposes if you are present in Ireland for: 183 days or more in a tax year or 280 days or more in total, taking the current tax year plus the preceding tax year together.

fact_text: You will not be tax resident in Ireland if present for 30 days or less in a tax year.
evidence_quote: You will not be resident in Ireland if you are here for 30 days or less in a tax year.

fact_text: If resident and domiciled in Ireland for tax purposes, you are chargeable to Irish tax on your worldwide income.
evidence_quote: If you are resident and domiciled in Ireland for tax purposes, you are chargeable to tax in Ireland on your worldwide income.

fact_text: Irish income tax has two rates, 20% (standard) and 40% (higher); for 2026 a single person has a standard rate band of €44,000 per year.
evidence_quote: A tax rate band is the amount of income which will be taxed at a particular percentage (tax rate). The current tax rates are 20% and 40%.

fact_text: For 2026 a single person's standard rate band (income taxed at 20%) is €44,000 per year, with income above taxed at 40%.
evidence_quote: Because Ann is single, she has a standard rate band of €44,000 per year.

fact_text: USC is a tax on total income; if total income exceeds €13,000 you pay USC on your full income.
evidence_quote: If your total income exceeds €13,000, you pay USC on your full income.

fact_text: Standard USC rates for 2026 are 0.5% on the first €12,012, 2% on the next €16,688, 3% on the next €41,344, and 8% on the balance.
evidence_quote: Standard rates and thresholds of USC for 2026 Threshold for 2026Rate First €12,012 0.5% Next €16,688 2% Next €41,344 3% Balance 8%

fact_text: On taking up a job an EU worker needs a PPS number and must register with Revenue; the employer then deducts PAYE, USC and PRSI.
evidence_quote: When you are offered a job, or if you want to start your own business, you will need to get a Public Personal Services Number (PPS number). You also must register with Revenue.

fact_text: Employees in industrial, commercial and service employment with reckonable pay of €38 or more per week are insured at PRSI Class A.
evidence_quote: people in industrial, commercial and service-type employment who are employed under a contract of service with reckonable pay of €38 or more per week from all employments

fact_text: For Class A earnings above €552 per week, the employee pays 4.20% and the employer 11.25% (up to 30 September 2026), rising to 4.35% employee and 11.40% employer from 1 October 2026.
evidence_quote: More than €552 A1 All 4.20 11.25

fact_text: The employer is responsible for deducting employee PRSI from pay and also pays separate employer PRSI contributions for employees aged 16 and over.
evidence_quote: Your employer is responsible for deducting PRSI from your pay. They also pay separate ‘employer PRSI contributions’ for employees aged 16 and over.

fact_text: Under EU coordination rules people usually pay social insurance in the country where they work, so a Spanish national working in Ireland pays PRSI in Ireland.
evidence_quote: People usually pay social insurance in the country where they work. For example, if a person works in Ireland, they pay social insurance (PRSI) in Ireland.

fact_text: A worker posted temporarily within the EU keeps paying social insurance in the sending country and uses an A1 Certificate to prove it; a Spanish employee posted to Ireland would remain in the Spanish system under a Spanish A1.
evidence_quote: If you are going to work in Europe for a short time, you need an A1 Certificate (formerly E101 Form) to show where you will pay your social insurance.

fact_text: Social insurance contributions made in another EEA country (e.g. Spain) can be combined with Irish contributions to qualify for Irish benefits.
evidence_quote: You can combine social insurance contributions that you made in another EEA country to qualify for Irish benefits.

fact_text: Everyone ordinarily resident in Ireland is entitled to public health services free or at reduced cost; ordinary residence means living in Ireland for at least a year or intending to for at least one year.
evidence_quote: Everyone ordinarily resident in Ireland and certain visitors to Ireland are entitled to a range of public health services either free of charge or at reduced cost. You are ordinarily resident if you have been living in Ireland for at least a year or you intend to live here for at least one year.

fact_text: Any person, regardless of nationality, accepted by the HSE as ordinarily resident is entitled to full eligibility (Category 1, medical card) or limited eligibility (Category 2).
evidence_quote: Any person, regardless of nationality, who is accepted by the HSE as being ordinarily resident in Ireland is entitled to either full eligibility (Category 1, medical card holders) or limited eligibility (Category 2) for health services.

fact_text: Without a medical card or GP visit card you are not entitled to free GP services (limited eligibility patients pay for GP visits).
evidence_quote: If you do not have a medical card or a GP visit card, you are not entitled to free GP services.

fact_text: A person working in Ireland and liable to pay PRSI is assessed for a means-tested medical card rather than a medical card under EU pensioner/insured-elsewhere rules.
evidence_quote: You must not be in receipt of a contributory Irish social welfare payment or be working in Ireland and be liable to pay PRSI. If you are working in Ireland, you may qualify for a means tested medical card.

fact_text: An EHIC covers access to public healthcare in another EU/EEA state for a temporary stay of up to 3 months and does not cover ongoing or permanent healthcare — so it bridges only the transition, not settled residence in Ireland.
evidence_quote: The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) allows you to access public healthcare in another EU/EEA state for free or at a reduced rate. You can use it when you are travelling abroad or when you are staying temporarily in another EU State.
